actions.justification: Mandatory action. Patient has severely elevated MAP of 160 mmHg with symptoms of severe headache and blurred vision suggesting hypertensive emergency. Formal BP assessment is required immediately.

Mandatory action. Comprehensive vital sign assessment is required to establish baseline and detect any hemodynamic instability or other abnormalities in this patient presenting with possible hypertensive emergency.

Mandatory action. Critical to determine if this is a hypertensive emergency (with end-organ damage) vs. urgency. Patient has neurological symptoms (headache, blurred vision) and CKD stage 3 making end-organ assessment essential.

Patient presents with severe headache and blurred vision with MAP of 160 mmHg, suggesting hypertensive emergency. Neurological assessment is critical to evaluate for hypertensive encephalopathy, stroke, or other CNS involvement as part of end-organ damage evaluation.
Continuous BP monitoring is essential in hypertensive emergency to track response to treatment and guide titration of antihypertensive therapy. MAP of 160 requires close surveillance.
Patient has CKD stage 3 with hypertensive emergency. Monitoring urine output is critical to assess for hypertensive nephropathy and renal end-organ damage, and to guide fluid management.

Severe headache with blurred vision and hypertensive emergency requires urgent CT head to rule out intracranial hemorrhage, hypertensive encephalopathy, or stroke before any further intervention. Critical for diagnosis.
Chest X-ray is part of hypertensive emergency workup to assess for aortic dissection, pulmonary edema, or cardiac enlargement as signs of end-organ damage.

Neurological symptoms (severe headache, blurred vision) in the setting of hypertensive emergency warrant urgent neurology consultation for co-management and assessment of hypertensive encephalopathy or other intracranial pathology.

Patient has CKD stage 3 and hypertensive emergency. BMP is essential to assess renal function (creatinine, BUN), electrolytes, and glucose to guide antihypertensive choice and monitor end-organ damage.

Severe headache and blurred vision with MAP of 160 mmHg raises concern for hypertensive encephalopathy or posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES). MRI brain (without gadolinium given CKD stage 3) is indicated to evaluate for PRES, stroke, or other intracranial pathology after CT head already completed.
ECG is indicated in hypertensive emergency to assess for left ventricular hypertrophy, ischemic changes, or arrhythmia as part of end-organ damage workup.
CBC is essential to evaluate for signs of infection, anemia, or thrombocytopenia that could contribute to hypertensive emergency or end-organ damage. Not yet completed.
Patient has CKD stage 3; eGFR needed to assess current renal function and guide antihypertensive drug selection (e.g., avoid nephrotoxic agents). Not yet completed.
Coagulation studies are warranted given severe headache and hypertensive emergency to rule out coagulopathy that could complicate management or indicate thrombotic microangiopathy.

Urinalysis is essential in this patient with hypertension, CKD stage 3, and suspected hypertensive emergency. Proteinuria and hematuria on UA would confirm renal end-organ damage and guide management. This is a key diagnostic step not yet completed.

Troponin should be ordered to evaluate for cardiac end-organ damage in this suspected hypertensive emergency. Elevated troponin would indicate hypertensive heart damage and influence treatment urgency and targets.

Given CKD stage 3 as a comorbidity and concern for hypertensive nephropathy/emergency, nephrology consultation is appropriate to guide safe antihypertensive targets and protect residual renal function during treatment.

Patient with hypertensive emergency (MAP ~160, neurological symptoms including severe headache and blurred vision) requires ICU-level monitoring for continuous BP monitoring and safe titration of IV antihypertensives.
